findings.desc: doc-promise-undelivered: packages/main/src/cli-engine.ts:1216-1221 (writeCodexProcessEvent) excludes ONLY entry.command==="quorum_submit" from the generic post-handler codex_cli process-event append, with a comment stating this is because quorum_submit "owns one exact immutable process-events transaction inside its handler" and a generic append "would make that canonical commit dirty again". quorum_prune (packages/main/src/handlers/quorum-prune.ts:20-22,338-365) commits process-events.jsonl through the IDENTICAL captureLifecycleMetadataTransaction/commitLifecycleMetadataTransaction machinery and its own header comment explicitly claims parity ("committed through the SAME lifecycle-metadata transaction machinery quorum_submit uses so the pre-dirty refusal, exact-content verification, and rollback all hold") — a claim also repeated in command-policy.ts:480 and process-fact-levels.ts:209, both touched by this diff. cli-engine.ts was NOT updated to add the matching exclusion for quorum_prune. Live repro (built dist, temp git fixture, LATTICE_ACTIVITY_SOURCE=codex): `lattice quorum_prune --apply` succeeds and commits cleanly (HEAD advances, applied:true), but immediately after, `git status --porcelain` shows `M .lattice/story/actives/<id>/process-events.jsonl` — the exact file quorum_prune just atomically committed is re-dirtied by the unguarded generic codex_cli append, which is the precise poisoning mode the sibling comment for quorum_submit exists to prevent. This leftover dirty state then makes quorum_prune/quorum_submit pre-dirty-refuse on the very next call for reasons unrelated to genuine story changes. No test in packages/main/src/tasks/quorum-submit-smoke.ts exercises `quorum_prune --apply` through the real CLI (runFixtureCli, which sets LATTICE_ACTIVITY_SOURCE=codex) with a post-command git-status-clean assertion (unlike the existing quorum_submit CLI test at line ~939 which does assert `git status --porcelain=v1===`), so this gap is untested. WHY: the diff repeatedly promises quorum_prune has transactional parity with quorum_submit including pre-dirty-refusal integrity, but the one cross-file wiring point that actually protects that guarantee under Codex-driven sessions was left half-registered.

handlers/quorum-prune.ts:125-135 writeUniqueBackup() writes the pre-prune backup directly into the git-tracked story dir (.lattice/story/actives/<id>/process-events.jsonl.bak-<ts>) and NEVER stages/commits/gitignores it (no matching *.bak-* gitignore pattern; the *.bak pattern at .gitignore does not match the .bak-<timestamp> suffix). Verified live: after `quorum_prune {apply:true}` succeeds, `git status --porcelain=v1 --untracked-files=all` in the story dir shows `?? .../process-events.jsonl.bak-<ts>` (repro output captured). Both assertCleanPruneBaseline (quorum-prune.ts:112-123, called at :336) and assertCleanQuorumBaseline (quorum-submit.ts:219-228, called at :529) do a raw whole-tree `git status --porcelain=v1 --untracked-files=all` with zero exemption for this file, so the very first legitimate follow-up action after a successful recovery -- another quorum_prune apply, OR a genuinely-new quorum_submit once the story-owned files change -- throws "worktree/index must be clean"/"nothing to prune" refusals caused entirely by the tool's own leftover backup, not by real user dirt. The same unexempted --untracked-files=all pattern is reused broadly (validation-executor.ts:202, done-prepare-generated-metadata.ts:362, dirty-worktree-gate.ts:42, recover-evidence.ts:68, cross-host-review.ts:81), so a leftover backup can also block TEST/DONE-adjacent gates. This directly undermines the story's stated goal ("the escalation floor returns to the pre-poisoning assurance level" / official low-friction recovery) since the operator must now manually discover and clean up (commit, delete, or gitignore) the tool's own artifact before doing anything else in the story. None of the 12 quorum_prune smoke checks catch this: the one test that runs quorum_prune apply twice ("never overwrites a previous run backup") masks it by doing its own `git add -A; git commit` between the two applies, which incidentally absorbs the first backup file into a commit -- a step a real operator/recovery workflow would not necessarily perform.
